source_refs.note: Exercise 4.1, Question 3: temperature of a body losing heat, surroundings negligible; book p. 128, answers p. 303 (PDF 305)

blocks.prompt: 3 Let \(T\) denote the temperature of a body at time \(t\). Suppose that the effect of the surrounding medium is negligible. Construct a differential equation that represents the temperature of the body at any time \(t\), assuming the body is losing heat due to some internal processes.
blocks.explanation:
A modelling question about cooling with no surroundings.
As in all such models we assume the rate of change of \(T\) is proportional to \(T\); losing heat means \(T\) decreases, so the rate is negative.
steps:
Given: temperature \(T(t)\); surroundings have no effect; the body is losing heat.
To find: a differential equation for \(T\).
Method: assume \(\frac{dT}{dt} \propto T\) and fix the sign from "losing heat".

Write the proportionality
\[\dfrac{dT}{dt} \propto T\]
Why: a hotter body loses heat faster; with no surroundings to compare with, the rate depends on \(T\) itself.

Fix the sign
The body is losing heat, so \(T\) decreases and \(\frac{dT}{dt} < 0\). With a positive constant \(k\):
\[\dfrac{dT}{dt} = -kT\]
\[\dfrac{dT}{dt} + kT = 0,\quad k > 0\]
Why: \(T > 0\) and \(k > 0\) make \(-kT\) negative, which is exactly "losing heat".

Check:
Newton's law \(\frac{dT}{dt} = k(T_{S} - T)\) with the surroundings switched off (\(T_{S} = 0\)) gives the same \(\frac{dT}{dt} = -kT\). Also \(T = T_{0}e^{-kt}\) satisfies it (sympy). The key prints \(\frac{dT}{dt} + kT = 0,\ k > 0\). Agrees.
